accuracy.evidence: Follows the KS3 science wording (forces as pushes or pulls, using force arrows in diagrams, adding forces in one dimension, balanced and unbalanced forces) and the Year 5 statement that forces are measured in newtons. Every number was checked on the 1 square = 10 N grid: a 20 N weight balanced by a 20 N table push, a 40 N push drawn 4 squares long, 50 - 30 = 20 N right in the tug of war, 30 + 20 = 50 N for two pushes the same way, and 40 N pedal against 40 N air resistance giving steady speed.

misconceptions.evidence: Targets the Aristotelian idea that a moving object needs a resultant force to keep moving (the bike keeps going at steady speed once forces balance), the belief that tables and shelves cannot push, adding forces that act in opposite directions, and reading arrow length as the number of newtons instead of squares times 10. The adult notes name these as common mistakes and link the bike step to Newton's first law.

lab_distinct.evidence: flagfdiag is a free-body diagram builder on squared paper: the object is a 2 by 2 square box and the child drags arrow tips to set each force to scale, plus a dashed resultant arrow, and a moving bike with live speeding up, steady or slowing down physics. It passes the 30% shingle gate and is unlike the other science labs, which use circuits, particles, food chains and sorting cards rather than scaled vectors.

lab_teaches.evidence: Five build steps each add one idea on the same grid: balance a weight with a reaction push, draw a force to scale, find the resultant of opposite forces by subtracting, find it for same-way forces by adding, then see that balanced forces on a moving bike mean constant speed rather than stopping. The Challenge then asks the same ideas with a shelf, friction on a box, a car, sledge dogs and a ball.

predictions.evidence: Four of the five build steps ask a prediction first: what the table does under a 20 N book, how many squares a 40 N push needs, the resultant of a 30 N and 50 N tug of war, and what a moving bike does when the forces become equal. The distractors are the real wrong ideas (tables cannot push, 80 N by adding, the bike stops), so a wrong pick exposes the misconception before the drag.

challenge_feedback.evidence: Six Challenge questions, each wrong answer tagged with its own reason in why(): no push from the shelf, doubling the push, adding opposite forces, pointing the resultant the wrong way, misreading the scale, thinking motion needs a force, speeding up without an unbalanced force, and subtracting same-way forces. Right answers count a streak, and a three-line rule card sits above the questions.

readability.evidence: Kid paragraphs score about Flesch-Kincaid grade 1.3, using push, pull, arrow, squares and balanced in short sentences. The adult notes come out at grade 4.4 after rewriting into short sentences, while still quoting the curriculum phrases. Step text is two short sentences, and labels on the canvas give the force name and size, such as Table push 20 N, with a halo so grid lines never cut the words.

no_filler.evidence: Each paragraph carries content: the kid text covers what an arrow shows, the scale, balanced and unbalanced, and adding or taking away. The adult text gives the curriculum link, the named mistakes, what each lab step shows and a family tip with a toy car slowed by friction and a book held on a hand, sketched to scale. The content gate found no stock phrases, and similarity to other lessons is under 12%.

mobile.evidence: Screenshots at the iPhone 13 viewport in light and dark show the grid, box, arrows and labels fit inside the canvas with no sideways scroll; horizontal labels sit beside the arrow from the box edge and vertical labels clear the drag ring. The plus and minus 10 N buttons are large, and the browser walk passed on desktop and phone with five steps and three completed tasks.

accessibility.evidence: Every drag has a button twin (minus or plus 10 N, and left or right 10 N for the resultant) with aria-labels, and say() updates the canvas aria-label and live caption with the words, for example 'Resultant 20 N to the right: 50 take away 30'. Each arrow is named and labelled with its size, so colour is never the only cue, and axe found no issues in either theme.
